chapter: Piron, Clarence Williams and the ODJB repertoire
title: Black-composed numbers the ODJB featured and how the band sang them
summary: La Rocca says he meant no harm to Black composers; the band featured Brown Skin, Mama's Baby Boy and Sister Kate, shouted them rather than sang, and played tunes by both Black and white writers.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: What we played: tunes and repertoire in the early days

blocks.x: Well this will show that I did try to help the colored man out, and I had no malice or thought of doing anybody anything that was out of the way of being honest with anyone. We featured these numbers that rise to others. We featured Brown Skin, Who You Follow, which Will Rossiter published. That's one of his numbers. We featured Mama's Baby Boy. Now, it's been said that we played many Negro melodies. That is true. Because we played many other tunes. Let me get back. And we also featured Sister Kate. It was all of the three of them. We had special arrangements on them. We used to get up. We didn't sing, but we used to holler, sing like we were trying to sing. In other words, it pleased the public. They liked what we were doing. And they'd ask for the same things over, and we'd play it.
Who did the singing of the band?

Five of us. You know what I mean? Yeah. I'd get up there and start, I wish I could Jimmy like my sister Kate. Da-da-da-da, da-da-da-da, da-da-da. And so on. It says, Mama's Baby Boy. Da-da-da-da-da-da-da. There were good numbers. And we played them. The same as some of these days. Downtown Strutters Ball. Or many other tunes that was owned by colored people we played. From that, all the people write about us, they said they played colored melodies. Sure, we played colored melodies. We also played melodies that were written by white people. But we didn't sing to white people's melodies. You don't ask me why? I don't know. Because they were made different. In other words, when we got out there, who you for? Brown skin, I'm for you white folks. Stuff like that. That would appeal to the northern man. But I'd get out there somewhere, and I'd have to have a good voice to sing that. You understand? It was more of a more popular tune. And we weren't going out there and saying something that everybody sang. Because we'd be making fools out of ourselves. We'd sound like a bunch of bullfrogs. Singing against a man that could sing. And these other tunes, we didn't need much voice to sing them. And we made them popular. Now this was between the years of 1921, 1919. In 21 and 22, Sister Kate. We sang that at Top and Wagey Garden. That's when we made that popular. Around 21 or 1920. But the others were prior to that. Now he had sent me these tunes. From time to time, he'd send me numbers. I had never known of Clarence Williams in my life. But Clarence Williams in the orchestra world in 1936, he has an article in the orchestra world. It says, From Honky Tongue to Swing. An interview by Clarence Williams. Well, this is a kind of long article.
